title: Head on the arm
hookLine: a quiet prayer of confession, head resting on the arm, left out on happy days
last: LET MY SOUL BE LIKE DUST.

lines: HEADS DOWN, LIKE STUDENTS AT DESKS.
cards: A weekday morning service, a minute after the Amidah ends, can look like a room full of tired students.
People sit down, lean forward, and rest their foreheads on their forearms, like a kid with their head down on the desk. The room goes quiet. Nobody's asleep.
They're saying a prayer that's meant to be said from that low place. And on some days, the happiest ones, the whole thing is simply skipped.

teach.h: FROM FALLING ON THE FACE TO THE ARM.
teach.b: Its oldest form is nefilat apayim, falling on the face. In the Bible, Moses and Aaron fall on their faces before God; so does Joshua, after a defeat.
In the time of the Talmud, people seem to have stretched out on the ground.
Today, in many Ashkenazi communities, it's become the head resting on the arm; many Sephardi communities say it sitting, without lowering the head. The words are honest and low.

One line, from King David, is said in many communities just before. In the old Jewish translation: "let us fall now into the hand of the LORD; for His mercies are great; and let me not fall into the hand of man."
David has done wrong and is given a choice of punishments.

teach.h: INTO GOD'S HANDS, NOT HUMAN HANDS.
teach.b: He chooses God's hands over human hands, because, he says, His mercies are great. Then, in the Ashkenazi rite, Psalm 6: I am weary with my groaning. Here's the surprising part.
Tachanun is left out on joyful days: Shabbat and festivals, the new month, Hanukkah and Purim, the whole month of Nisan.
When there's a groom in the room in the week after his wedding, or a father whose baby is having his bris that day.

Even, strangely, on the fast of Tisha b'Av, because a verse in Lamentations calls that day a mo'ed, an appointed time, the same word used for a festival. Head down on ordinary weekdays; head up on the days marked for joy.

how: On ordinary weekdays, after the morning and afternoon Amidah, many Jews say Tachanun, in many Ashkenazi communities resting the head on the forearm; it is omitted on Shabbat, festivals, Rosh Chodesh, Hanukkah, Purim, all of Nisan, Tisha b'Av and in other joyful circumstances.

o: a song of praise sung on Shabbat
a fast day for mourning the Temple
supplication, said with the head down

p: fall into God's hands, not man's

s: Tachanun is said every day of the year
it's left out on Shabbat, festivals, Rosh Chodesh, Nisan and other joyful days.

games.q: you're King David. you've done wrong and must choose: fall into human hands, or into God's. what do you choose?
o: human hands; they're easier to bargain with.
God's hands, for His mercies are great.
games.why: let us fall now into the hand of the LORD; for His mercies are great; and let me not fall into the hand of man.

practice: If you're at a table or desk, lean forward and rest your forehead on your forearm; if not, just lower your head and let your shoulders drop.

From down there, say one honest thing, where you fell short this week or what you're tired of carrying, without arguing with it or fixing it. If you pray, you can say it into God's hands, then sit up slowly when you're ready.

wordCard.voice: Tachanun. Supplication. The prayer after the Amidah, said with the head down on the arm, and left out on joyful days.

orig.note: Hebrew: supplication, pleading. from the root ch-n-n, grace, favor.

carryVoice: Your line: low and honest. Some words are best said from the low place. See you tomorrow.
